key_terms.meaning: Partial molar Gibbs energy of component i, μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ) at fixed T, P and other n; at phase equilibrium it is equal in every phase present.
The 'corrected pressure' that replaces partial pressure in real systems, defined by μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(fᵢ/fᵢ°); equal fugacity in all phases is the working form of phase equilibrium.
Ratio φᵢ = fᵢ/(yᵢP) in a vapour or fᵢ/(xᵢP) in a liquid; φᵢ → 1 as P → 0 for a gas.
Dimensionless fugacity ratio aᵢ = fᵢ/fᵢ°, where fᵢ° is the fugacity of the component in a chosen standard state, usually pure liquid at the same T and P.
All phases in contact share one temperature T and one pressure P; otherwise heat or volume flows and the state is not equilibrium.
A phase is stable only if its Gibbs energy is at a minimum, i.e. (∂²G/∂x²)T,P > 0; a negative curvature means the mixture splits into two phases.
A physically distinct and mechanically separable part of the system, such as one liquid layer, a vapour, or a solid crystal.
The smallest number of independent chemical species needed to describe the composition of every phase of the system.
The number of intensive variables (T, P, compositions) that can be fixed independently without changing the number of phases present.
F = C − P + 2, with C = number of components, P = number of phases, and 2 standing for temperature and pressure.
For any closed system of known overall composition, fixing any two independent intensive variables fixes the entire intensive state, whatever the number of phases and components.
At a given liquid composition, the bubble point is the T (or P) at which the first vapour bubble appears; at a given vapour composition, the dew point is where the first liquid drop appears.
Plots of equilibrium pressure (or temperature) against liquid mole fraction x and vapour mole fraction y for a binary; the two curves meet only at pure components or at an azeotrope.
yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, where Pᵢˢᵃᵗ is the pure-component vapour pressure at the same T; valid for ideal solutions and near-ideal components.
yᵢP = xᵢγᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, adding the liquid-phase activity coefficient γᵢ to correct for real-solution non-ideality in the liquid.
γᵢ = aᵢ/xᵢ; it measures how far the liquid mixture is from ideal, γᵢ = 1 meaning ideal and γᵢ > 1 meaning positive deviation from Raoult's law.
The slope of the solute fugacity against its own mole fraction in the limit xᵢ → 0: fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ, with Hᵢ having units of pressure.
For high-pressure VLE both phases use one equation of state: yᵢφᵢ^V = xᵢφᵢ^L, so no activity coefficient appears.
Kᵢ = yᵢ/xᵢ, the ratio of mole fractions at equilibrium; for Raoult's law Kᵢ = Pᵢˢᵃᵗ/P and for modified Raoult's law Kᵢ = γᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ/P.
A line joining the compositions of two phases that are in equilibrium with each other, for example the two liquid layers in extraction.

takeaways: At phase equilibrium every phase has the same T, the same P, and the same chemical potential (hence the same fugacity) for every component.
A phase exists only where the Gibbs energy is a minimum; a concave region of the Gibbs energy curve forces the mixture to split into two phases.
The phase rule F = C − P + 2 counts the intensive variables you may set freely; Duhem's theorem says a closed system needs only two.
For a pure component the equality of chemical potentials reduces to equality of pure-phase fugacities, which defines the vapour-pressure curve.
Raoult's law yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ is the starting point for every VLE calculation; real systems need only γᵢ added.
In a very dilute solution the solute follows Henry's law fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ, not Raoult's law, because its environment is solvent, not itself.
At high pressure the liquid is also compressible and non-ideal, so both phases are described by fugacity coefficients from an equation of state.
The same fugacity equality applied to two liquid phases gives liquid-liquid extraction; applied to a solid and a solution it gives the solubility curve.
bank_note: Long answers are built around the single fugacity-equality statement, then carried through the phase rule, Duhem's theorem, Raoult's and modified Raoult's law with bubble/dew calculations, Henry's law, and the high-pressure φ-φ and liquid-liquid/solid-liquid cases.

bank.q: State the conditions required for phase equilibrium between two phases of a multi-component system. Explain why equality of temperature and pressure is necessary, and why equality of chemical potential is the complete condition.
outline: Thermal equilibrium: no heat flow, so Tᵢ = T across phases.
Mechanical equilibrium: no work of volume change, so Pᵢ = P across phases.
For each component, dG = 0 at constant T and P gives μᵢ^α = μᵢ^β for every species i.
In fugacity form: fᵢ^α = fᵢ^β, which is what is actually used in calculations.
Mass transfer stops only when chemical potential is equal; T and P equality alone is not sufficient.

bank.q: Define fugacity, fugacity coefficient, activity and activity coefficient. Give the relation connecting them and state the standard states used for vapour and liquid phases.
outline: Fugacity fᵢ defined by μᵢ = μᵢ° + RT ln(fᵢ/fᵢ°); it has units of pressure and equals partial pressure as P → 0.
Fugacity coefficient φᵢ = fᵢ/(yᵢP) for vapour, fᵢ/(xᵢP) for liquid.
Activity aᵢ = fᵢ/fᵢ°; activity coefficient γᵢ = aᵢ/xᵢ.
Vapour standard state: ideal gas at 1 bar, giving fᵢ = φᵢyᵢP.
Liquid standard state: pure liquid at the same T and P, giving fᵢ = γᵢxᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ after the Poynting correction is dropped.

bank.q: State the Gibbs phase rule and Duhem's theorem. Explain the meaning of each term in F = C − P + 2 and show with examples why Duhem's theorem is more useful than the phase rule for a closed system.
outline: C = components, P = phases, 2 = temperature and pressure; F = degrees of freedom.
Examples: one-component two-phase gives F = 1; two-component two-phase gives F = 2.
Duhem: for a closed system of fixed overall composition, any two independent intensive variables fix the whole intensive state.
Phase rule gives only the count F, while Duhem also holds when P > 2 and when composition changes with phases.
A binary VLE flash is fully specified by T and P even though F = 2 and the compositions are unknown until the equations are solved.

bank.q: Draw and explain the P-x-y and T-x-y diagrams for an ideal binary mixture. Define bubble point and dew point, and use the lever rule to find the amounts of the two phases.
outline: Bubble-point curve gives P (or T) against liquid composition x; dew-point curve against vapour composition y.
At a given T, the bubble pressure is the higher curve on a P-x-y diagram; the dew pressure lies below it.
Two-phase region lies between the curves; tie line joins equilibrium x and y at the same T and P.
Lever rule: (amount of vapour)/(amount of liquid) = (z − x)/(y − z), with z the overall mole fraction.
Azeotrope where the curves touch: x = y, and no separation by simple distillation.

bank.q: State Henry's law and compare it with Raoult's law for the solute and the solvent in a dilute binary solution. Explain why the solvent obeys Raoult's law while the solute obeys Henry's law in the same solution.
outline: Henry: fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ as xᵢ → 0, Hᵢ a constant with units of pressure.
Raoult: fᵢ = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, valid as xᵢ → 1.
Solvent molecules are surrounded mostly by solvent, so Raoult's law applies to the major component.
Solute molecules are surrounded by solvent, so their escaping tendency depends on solute-solvent forces, giving Hᵢ ≠ Pᵢˢᵃᵗ.
Both laws are limiting cases of the same fugacity-composition curve: slope Hᵢ at x → 0 and slope Pᵢˢᵃᵗ at x → 1.

bank.q: An ideal binary liquid mixture of A and B is at 350 K. Given the Antoine constants for both components, calculate the bubble-point pressure and the vapour composition for x_A = 0.4. Then calculate the dew-point pressure for y_A = 0.4.
outline: Use Antoine's equation to get P_Aˢᵃᵗ and P_Bˢᵃᵗ at 350 K, with T in K and P in the correct unit.
Bubble pressure: P = x_A P_Aˢᵃᵗ + x_B P_Bˢᵃᵗ.
Vapour composition: y_A = x_A P_Aˢᵃᵗ / P.
Dew pressure: P = 1/(y_A/P_Aˢᵃᵗ + y_B/P_Bˢᵃᵗ).
Check that Σyᵢ = 1 and that the dew pressure is lower than the bubble pressure at the same T.

bank.q: For a binary system whose liquid-phase activity coefficients are given by the two-parameter Margules equation, set up and solve the modified Raoult's law calculation for the bubble pressure and vapour composition at a given T and x.
outline: Write ln γ₁ and ln γ₂ from the Margules constants A₁₂ and A₂₁.
Calculate γ₁ and γ₂ at the given x₁.
P = x₁γ₁P₁ˢᵃᵗ + x₂γ₂P₂ˢᵃᵗ.
y₁ = x₁γ₁P₁ˢᵃᵗ/P; check y₁ + y₂ = 1.
Comment that γᵢ > 1 raises P above the ideal value and can produce a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

bank.q: The solubility of a sparingly soluble gas in water is required at 298 K and 5 bar partial pressure. Given Henry's constant for the gas in water, calculate the mole fraction dissolved and explain how the solubility changes with temperature and pressure.
outline: Apply fᵢ = Hᵢxᵢ with fᵢ taken as the gas partial pressure at low pressure.
xᵢ = Pᵢ/Hᵢ; quote the mole fraction in ppm if small.
Solubility rises linearly with partial pressure (Henry's law).
Hᵢ increases with temperature for gases of low solubility, so solubility falls as T rises.
Note the assumption: ideal gas phase and negligible Poynting correction.

bank.q: A binary mixture is to be flashed at 300 K and 20 bar. Outline the φ-φ calculation using a cubic equation of state, showing how the K-values are obtained and how the flash is converged.
outline: Choose an equation of state and mixing rules; get fugacity coefficients φᵢ from it.
Equilibrium: yᵢφᵢ^V = xᵢφᵢ^L, so Kᵢ = φᵢ^L/φᵢ^V.
Kᵢ depends on both compositions, so the calculation is iterative.
Rachford-Rice equation for the vapour fraction β, solved by Newton iteration.
Update compositions using new φ values; stop when successive K values agree within a small tolerance.

bank.q: Two partially miscible liquids A and B are in equilibrium. Using activity coefficients, set up the equations that give the compositions of the two coexisting liquid layers, and state how the tie lines are drawn on a triangular diagram.
outline: Equilibrium condition for each component: xᵢ^α γᵢ^α = xᵢ^β γᵢ^β, since pure-component standard states cancel.
Two such equations (one per component) with two unknown compositions.
Solution gives the binodal (coexistence) curve.
Tie lines join the two liquid compositions at equilibrium; they are not parallel in general.
Distribution coefficient Kᵢ = xᵢ^β/xᵢ^α = γᵢ^α/γᵢ^β; selectivity of extraction depends on it.

bank.q: Explain, with the Gibbs energy against composition curve, why a binary liquid mixture splits into two phases. Distinguish the binodal from the spinodal curve and state the stability condition.
outline: Plot Gmix against x₁ at constant T and P; a concave region means (∂²G/∂x₁²) < 0.
A single phase with a concave curve would lower its G by splitting into two phases.
Common tangent to the two minima gives the binodal (phase boundary) compositions.
Spinodal is where the curvature is zero; inside it the mixture is unstable and splits spontaneously.
Between binodal and spinodal the state is metastable; nucleation is needed.
Limiting case of the critical solution point where the two curves meet.

bank.q: A binary system at 1 atm shows a minimum-boiling azeotrope. Explain how this follows from the activity coefficients, how the phase rule applies at the azeotrope, and why ordinary distillation cannot separate it.
outline: Azeotrope means xᵢ = yᵢ, so from modified Raoult's law γᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ = P for each component.
A minimum-boiling azeotrope requires γᵢ > 1 (positive deviation from Raoult's law) and P above the ideal bubble pressure.
At the azeotrope the two curves touch; C = 2, P = 2 gives F = 1, so fixing T also fixes P and both compositions.
At the azeotropic composition the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so no enrichment occurs.
Use of a different solvent, pressure-swing or azeotropic distillation is needed.
Mention the Gibbs-Duhem consistency test on measured γ values before trusting the conclusion.

bank.q: Compare the γ-φ and φ-φ approaches to vapour-liquid equilibrium. For each approach, state the assumptions, the data required, the typical pressure range, and the kind of system where it fails.
outline: γ-φ: yᵢφᵢ^V P = xᵢγᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ, with φᵢ^V from a virial-type correlation and γᵢ from a liquid model.
γ-φ suits low to moderate pressure (roughly up to 10 bar) where the vapour is nearly ideal and the liquid standard state is well defined.
φ-φ: yᵢφᵢ^V = xᵢφᵢ^L, both coefficients from the same cubic equation of state with mixing rules.
φ-φ suits high pressure and supercritical components, where no pure liquid vapour pressure exists.
Failure of γ-φ: near the critical point, at very high pressure, and for supercritical gases.
Failure of φ-φ: polar and associating liquids near atmospheric pressure, where simple cubic equations give poor liquid densities.
Both reduce to the same fugacity-equality criterion derived in chapter 6.1.

bank.q: Duhem's theorem is stated for a closed system. Discuss how the intensive state of a vapour-liquid-liquid three-phase system is determined, and how the phase rule count and Duhem's theorem are reconciled.
outline: Write phase rule for C = 2, P = 3: F = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1.
Duhem: fixing T (say) fixes P and all three compositions, so one variable suffices.
Equations available: three phase-equilibrium equations (one per component per phase pair) plus the balance that overall composition lies on the triangle of the three phases.
For C components and P phases the number of independent equations equals the independent unknowns, which is why two variables always suffice for a closed system.
Practical consequence: a three-phase flash requires a very narrow range of T at fixed P, which is why the three-phase region appears as a line or a narrow band on diagrams.

bank.q: Solid A dissolves in liquid B. Derive the expression for the solubility of A in B from the fugacity-equality condition, and discuss why solubility rises with temperature when the heat of fusion is positive.
outline: Equilibrium: f_A^solid = f_A^solution.
Solid fugacity from the pure solid; solution fugacity written as γ_A x_A f_A° with f_A° the pure subcooled liquid.
Integrate the Gibbs-Helmholtz relation from the melting point T_m: ln(γ_A x_A) ≈ −(ΔH_fus/R)(1/T − 1/T_m).
For an ideal solution (γ_A = 1) this gives ln x_A = −(ΔH_fus/R)(1/T − 1/T_m).
With ΔH_fus > 0 the right side becomes less negative as T rises, so x_A increases with temperature.
Activity coefficient corrections matter for polar solutes and non-ideal solvents.

glossary.def: A state in which every phase has the same temperature and pressure and every component has the same chemical potential in every phase, so no net transfer occurs.
The partial molar Gibbs energy of a component, equal to the change in Gibbs energy when one mole of that component is added at constant T and P.
A pseudo-pressure that makes the ideal-gas chemical potential formula work for real fluids.
The ratio of a component's fugacity to its partial pressure, equal to 1 for an ideal gas.
The dimensionless ratio of a component's fugacity to its value in a chosen standard state.
The factor by which a component's behaviour in a mixture differs from ideal, equal to activity divided by mole fraction.
A solution in which every component obeys Raoult's law over the whole composition range and the heat of mixing is zero.
A defined reference state at the same temperature and pressure as the system, used to measure fugacity and activity; pure liquid is usual for liquids and ideal gas at 1 bar for vapours.
The relation F = C − P + 2 giving the number of intensive variables that can be set independently.
An independent chemical species needed to define the composition of all phases in the system.
One intensive variable that can be changed independently without changing the number of phases in equilibrium.
The statement that in a closed system of known overall composition, any two independent intensive variables fix the entire equilibrium state.
The temperature or pressure at which the first bubble of vapour forms in a liquid of given composition.
The temperature or pressure at which the first drop of liquid forms in a vapour of given composition.
A mixture whose liquid and vapour compositions are identical at equilibrium, so simple distillation cannot change its composition.
The ratio K₁/K₂ of the K-values of two components, which measures how easily they can be separated.
The relation yᵢP = xᵢPᵢˢᵃᵗ that describes vapour-liquid equilibrium for ideal solutions.
The relation that the solute fugacity in a very dilute solution is proportional to the solute mole fraction, with Henry's constant as the proportionality.
The slope of solute fugacity against solute mole fraction at infinite dilution, having units of pressure.
A mass-balance rule giving the relative amounts of two coexisting phases from the distances of the overall composition from the two phase compositions on a tie line.
A line joining the compositions of two phases that are in equilibrium with each other.
The boundary curve on a phase diagram, given by the common tangent construction, separating one-phase from two-phase behaviour.
The locus where the second derivative of Gibbs energy with composition is zero, marking the limit of spontaneous phase splitting.
The equilibrium ratio of the mole fractions of a component in two coexisting phases.
A small exponential factor that corrects liquid fugacity for pressure difference from the saturation pressure, usually near 1 at low pressure.
